history.heading: Hispania
paragraphs: The Iberian Peninsula has been inhabited for over a million years; the cave paintings of Altamira are masterpieces of Palaeolithic art. Iberians, Celts, Phoenicians, Greeks and Carthaginians lived there before Rome conquered Hispania, which became one of its most important provinces. Latin became the basis of Spanish, and emperors Trajan and Hadrian were born there.
The Visigoths ruled after the fall of Rome until 711, when Muslim forces from North Africa conquered most of the peninsula.

history.heading: Al-Andalus and the Reconquista
paragraphs: Muslim Al-Andalus flourished for centuries; Córdoba was one of the largest and most cultured cities in Europe, and the Alhambra in Granada is a jewel of Islamic architecture. Christian kingdoms in the north gradually expanded southward in the Reconquista.

The marriage of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon united Spain's main kingdoms. In 1492 they conquered Granada, expelled the Jews, and sponsored Christopher Columbus's voyage to the Americas.

history.heading: Empire and decline
paragraphs: In the 16th century Spain built a vast empire across the Americas, the Philippines and parts of Europe, enriched by American silver. Under Charles V and Philip II it was the dominant power in Europe. Spain's Golden Age produced Cervantes's Don Quixote and painters such as Velázquez and El Greco.
Spain declined in the 17th and 18th centuries, was invaded by Napoleon in 1808 and lost most of its American colonies by the 1820s, and its last major colonies in 1898.

history.heading: Civil war, Franco and democracy
paragraphs: The Second Republic, proclaimed in 1931, ended with the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939), won by General Francisco Franco's nationalists, who ruled as a dictatorship until his death in 1975. King Juan Carlos I then oversaw the transition to democracy, and a new constitution was adopted in 1978.

Spain joined NATO in 1982 and the European Community in 1986. The Basque terrorist group ETA ended its armed campaign in 2011. In 2017 a contested Catalan independence referendum caused a major political crisis. Felipe VI became king in 2014.

culture.heading: Languages and arts
paragraphs: Spanish (Castilian) is official nationwide, and Catalan, Basque (Euskara), Galician and others are co-official in their regions. Most Spaniards are Catholic by tradition, though practice has declined.

Spain has produced artists Goya, Picasso, Dalí and Miró, architect Antoni Gaudí (whose Sagrada Família in Barcelona is still being completed), filmmaker Pedro Almodóvar and many writers. Flamenco from Andalusia is recognised by UNESCO.

culture.heading: Food and festivals
paragraphs: Spanish cuisine includes tapas, paella, jamón ibérico, tortilla and gazpacho, and wines such as Rioja and sherry. Festivals include Semana Santa (Holy Week), Valencia's Fallas, Pamplona's San Fermín and La Tomatina. Football is a passion; Spain won the World Cup in 2010 and Real Madrid and Barcelona are among the world's biggest clubs. The women's team won the 2023 World Cup.

politics.heading: Parliamentary monarchy
paragraphs: Spain is a parliamentary monarchy. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Cortes Generales (Congress of Deputies and Senate). Spain is highly decentralised into 17 autonomous communities, some with strong regional identities and nationalist movements, especially Catalonia and the Basque Country.

Politics has fragmented beyond the traditional Socialist Party (PSOE) and conservative People's Party, with Vox, Sumar and regional parties. Pedro Sánchez of the PSOE has been prime minister since 2018.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Spain has the fourth-largest economy in the eurozone. Tourism is a major pillar; Spain is one of the most visited countries in the world. Other key sectors include cars, food and agriculture (olive oil, fruit, vegetables and wine), renewable energy, construction, banking and textiles (Inditex, owner of Zara).

Spain's economy grew faster than most of Europe after 2023. Persistent challenges include high unemployment, especially among young people, housing costs and regional differences. The currency is the euro.
